Back From Brazil - Gerhard Jansen van Vuuren

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
On the run for for almost 10 years, accused killer Gerhard Janse van Vuuren has finally been extradited from Brazil.

Unique Selling Point:
Chilling footage of the cold-blooded murder of 25-year-old Andrea Venter was broadcast on Carte Blanche in 2014. We interviewed the parents of the victim, a young accountant who was stalked, held captive, tortured and then brutally killed by her ex-boyfriend in full view of security cameras and witnesses at her townhouse complex in Fourways.
The video camera footage then showed how Gerhard Janse van Vuuren attempted to slit his own throat as he lay waiting to be apprehended.
They told how the justice system had failed Andrea at every turn: from the SAPS who ignored her appeals when Janse van Vuuren violated her Protection Order, to Judge Fritz van Oosten who released the accused on R15 000 bail when his case went on Appeal to the Johannesburg High Court. He then skipped bail and left the country on a false passport and disappeared in South America.

Summary:
The accused was subsequently arrested in Brazil for entering the country on a false passport, under the name Daniel Joseph Mouton. He was sentenced to 4 years and 4 months imprisonment, and SAPS attempted to have him extradited to face trial for murder. But Mouton was inexplicably released in 2016 after serving only 2 years.

Further information:
This story will re-visit the crime, and detail the investigation by ex-SAPS officials Gerard Labuschagne and JJ du Toit, together with Interpol, which finally brought the accused to justice and saw him return to South Africa to face trial. We see snippets of the new life created for himself in Rio de Janeiro with his new family.
We will review the charges against him, and chat to the Prosecutor, seasoned Advocate Paul Schutte.

Script:


BACK FROM BRAZIL

V/O: After 7 years on the run, murder accused Gerhard Jansen van Vuuren finally appears in the dock of the Johannesburg High Court. Shackled in leg irons he stares blankly ahead, as Judge Meshack Mabesele appoints a lawyer from Legal Aid to defend him. He is facing trial for the murder of his ex-girlfriend, 25-year-old accountant Andrea Venter.

Annatjie: She was for me a gift. She was a gift from God for me.

V/O: In 2014 Carte Blanche interviewed Andrea’s parents, Dries and Annetjie Venter. They described a violent relationship of emotional and physical abuse which ended in Andrea obtaining a Protection Order against Gerhard. That didn’t prevent him from stalking her and tracking her down to her flat in Fourways. In May 2011 he held her captive for an entire weekend.

Dries: He got hold of her and he did everything he wanted to. That blonde hair was pink with blood, this eyelid was cut open, her jaw was broken, her nose was broken.

Annatjie: In his flat was blood of her.

Dries: In his flat.

V/O: But early on Monday morning at Sibaya Sands CCTV footage shows she managed to escape from him and ran screaming to the guard house 150m away. Despite the neighbours and the guard going to investigate, nobody could intervene as van Vuuren chased her with a knife.

Annatjie: Yes and stabbed her from the back, stabbed her twelve times in the back.

V/O: The footage shows as Andrea reached the guard house van Vuuren slit her throat in front of everyone. He then stabbed himself in the neck before lying down next to her body and casually removing a belt he had tied around her neck. He threw the belt into the flower bed and then repositioned her body. With a crowd of onlookers gathered around he lay there with his hand covering his wound, waiting for the paramedics to arrive.

Link: This is where Andrea Venter’s life was taken with such shocking brutality in May 2011. It was captured on video. Eye-witnesses saw it happen, and the suspect was in custody. Justice should have been swift and certain. But that’s not what happened.
03:01:22
Gerard: The police successfully opposed bail twice in the Magistrate’s court. My report was one of the key elements in opposing bail.

V/O: In 2011, Dr Gerard Labuschagne was a police Brigadier in charge of the Investigative Psychology unit.
Gerard: You have a person who breaks the rules. You give them a set of rules like a Protection Order and he ignores them. Therefore, if you give them a set of rules in terms of bail instructions, he’s going to ignore them most likely.

V/O: Jansen van Vuuren took his bail application on appeal to the Johannesburg High Court, where he was finally granted bail.

Gerard: So I think there are multiple examples of where the justice system failed Andrea Venter before the murder and after the murder.

V/O: Gerhard’s parents divorced when he was 2. Gerhard Snr supported him in court. But once on bail, he went to live with his mother Thea Pretorius.

Thea: Gerhard is a product of gender violence. He grew up with his father and he never really were taught respect towards women.

V/O: Thea left her abusive marriage when she felt her life was in danger. But that meant Gerhard’s world view was shaped by his late father.

Thea: He admitted to me one day that he was still in primary school and he was addicted to pornography because his father had it all around in the house. And he said to me Mom, my father used to beat me so violently all the time that in the end pain became pleasure for me. How distorted!

V/O: After 18 months of freedom, Jansen van Vuuren skipped bail and left the country.

Thea: I knew he was going to skip the country, and me and his father helped him with certain things. His father took him through the night before he was supposed to appear in court, took him to Durban, and he flew from Durban.

V/O; He boarded an Emirates flight at King Shaka International airport and flew to Brazil via Dubai.

Claire: What did you help him with?

Thea: He needed a passport. So he had a friend, I think he paid him R5000 to get a passport in his name. And eventually I said why don’t you just give one of your photographs to be added on the passport and see if it’s going to work. So they did it and in the end he got the passport.

Claire: Why were you ok with that?

Thea: I’ve got no excuse for that. I’m just a mother, and unfortunately afterwards I felt very guilty about it.

Gerard: I think the mother - obviously dealing with the difficulties of being a mother, but also being an upstanding citizen - then did contact me and say she has information as to where he’d gone. And that information was crucial for us to be able to convey that to the Brazilian police.

V/O: In 2013 Advocate JJ du Toit was Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions in charge of extradition. Before that, he’d spent 17 years in The Hague at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, working alongside Judge Richard Goldstone. Experienced in extraditing war criminals, he now turned his attention to Jansen van Vuuren.

JJ: So we prepared the papers; we had a warrant and we had DNA and we had all these passports, because at the time we already knew that he had another name: he used Daniel Mouton for example.

V/O: Brazil granted the extradition request and Jansen van Vuuren was arrested in Rio de Janeiro in August 2013. But he was sentenced to 2-years imprisonment for entering the country on a false passport and had to complete that sentence before being returned to South Africa. Inexplicably, he was released in 2015 without being extradited.

JJ: Allegedly there was a judge that came into the prison and said this man has served his sentence and he should be released. So the head of the prison said but that cannot happen because he’s got a pending case to be extradited to South Africa. And they said no, he must be released. Unfortunately up ‘til today we don’t know the true reason why that happened. But he was freed again, and that was devastating, I must admit.

Dries: That made me furious, because they should have handed him over to Interpol and Interpol should have brought him to South Africa and it was never done.

V/O: Dries Venter still lives in Rustenburg. His wife Annetjie passed away in 2016 and he’s since remarried, but his life is consumed with seeking justice for Andrea.
The accused simply disappeared into a country of 200 million people. Interpol followed every lead but couldn’t trace him, and after 5 years it seemed he would get away with it. But this year there was a breakthrough.

Thea: During this year I went on Facebook and Gerhard got a hold of me via Facebook. And he phoned me. and then he told me about the little girl he had and she turned one year old in September now.

V/O; He told his wife he was from the Netherlands, and never mentioned the murder charges. He seemed so comfortable in his new role as a family man, that he forgot he was also a wanted man.

Gerard: We always say that the every contact leaves a trace and that’s normally referring to physical touch you know the police can find some evidence but it also refers to digital information. So whenever there was movement perhaps on social media or on phone calls or WhatsApp messages, there was always an attempt to try and follow those up.


V/O: Through meticulous detective work they traced the accused to an address in the Favelas of Rio de Janeiro.

JJ: It was really good intelligence that our police and the Interpol guys and the Brazilian police followed up and, you know they did their homework very, very well before they moved in. They went also at night to make sure that he is at the place, not to tip him off and that type of thing. They opened the door, he was there with his wife and his little kid. They in fact sent me the photos and I was so pleased when I saw that.

V/O: He was arrested on the 18th of June by the Brazilian Federal police and held in custody at the Department’s Headquarters. Four members of South Africa’s Interpol unit then collected him in Rio de Janeiro and escorted him back to OR Tambo, where he was greeted by more police and the media.

Link: The wheels of justice are about to turn full circle. After 7 years on the run Jansen van Vuuren is back at the Johannesburg High Court to face the music. This time there’ll be no escape.

V/O: His pre-trial hearing is set for the 27th of November, and Dries will be there to give him this letter.

Dries: My wife passed away from the heartbreak that you caused by killing Andrea. Actually, you are also responsible for my wife’s death. In other words, two murders!

Claire: Has he ever mentioned Andrea’s name, has he ever shown remorse for killing her?

Thea: No, he’s never shown remorse, not that I know of. It really was as if he thinks that that’s what she deserved.

V/O: Equally worrying are recent threats he allegedly made when his mother visited him in the Randburg Police cells.

Thea: It’s still my child, I cannot throw him away. But the way that he was really that day sitting there and telling me: if I get out of here - everybody of you people that are involved in this, that want to see me now going to jail – when I get there, I will kill everybody. I will take them all out. And he told me that he will take me out.

Claire: What do you think would be an appropriate sentence?

Thea: Life.

Claire: Life imprisonment?

Thea: Life in prison.

He was sentenced to 4 years and 4 months imprisonment, and SAPS attempted to have him extradited to face trial for murder. But Mouton was inexplicably released in 2016 after serving only 2 years.
metadata.Further information: This story will re-visit the crime, and detail the investigation by ex-SAPS officials Gerard Labuschagne and JJ du Toit, together with Interpol, which finally brought the accused to justice and saw him return to South Africa to face trial. We see snippets of the new life created for himself in Rio de Janeiro with his new family. We will review the charges against him, and chat to the Prosecutor, seasoned Advocate Paul Schutte.
